title: 7 Patterns That Derail Product Teams
intro: Written for PMs, engineers and stakeholders working with UXers: teams think they're debating a design when they're debating the goal, the constraints and what counts as evidence.

learn.title: The seven patterns
learn.text:
**1.** A screen change treated as a decision — “redesign” isn't a goal
**2.** Research as a vending machine — a Friday deadline doesn't recruit the right users
**3.** Opinions versus evidence — label what's observed, inferred and unknown
**4.** “Bias” heard as an insult — it's a predictable feature of thinking; ask which one
**5.** Speed versus confidence — how much weight can this finding carry?
**6.** The wrong slice of users — champions and power users aren't typical users
**7.** Shared goals left unstated — agree the goal before judging the screen

try.q: A stakeholder hears “that's a bias” as a personal criticism. What's the better framing?
options: Everyone has biases, so it doesn't matter
try.explain: It's a feature of thinking, not an accusation. Which one is this?.

learn.title: What the UXer's question is really doing
learn.text:
“What are we trying to accomplish?” isn't pushback. It prevents the team from locking into a solution before agreeing on the goal, the constraints and what counts as evidence.

Most of the seven patterns are the same conversation underneath: **what decision, what evidence, how sure.**

try.q: What are most of the seven patterns really about?
options: What decision, what evidence, how sure
How much time the research is going to take
try.explain: The same conversation in different disguises.

learn.title: How stakeholders can help
learn.text:
**Describe problems in verbs and consequences:** “people abandon after the fee summary, which creates calls” — not “the fee page needs a redesign”.

**Ask the UXer** what they directly observed, what they're inferring, and what evidence carries the most weight.

**Treat recruiting concerns as protection** against false confidence, not as perfectionism.

try.q: How should a stakeholder describe a problem?
try.explain: “People abandon after the fee summary, which creates calls.”

test.q: Who is the article written for?
test.explain: It explains the UXer's questions from the other side.

test.q: What is wrong with “research as a vending machine”?
options: A deadline doesn't recruit the right users
The vending-machine metaphor implies low quality
test.explain: Timeline pressure is applied to the part that can't compress.

test.q: What three labels help separate opinion from evidence?
test.explain: It makes the basis of a claim explicit.

test.q: Why are champion users a problem?
options: They refuse to criticise the product
test.explain: Studying the wrong slice produces confident, wrong findings.

options: How much weight can this finding carry?
How fast can we run the study?
When will the results actually be ready?
test.explain: A fast study can still be useful if its limits are known.
